And that is the whole answer. No third sentence.
Three things, and I will be direct. The margin fell, you left without another role, and you have never worked outside Brazil. Start wherever you like.
There are three parts to that. I will take them in your order.
Good.
Although the margin fell in those two years, the cash position improved every quarter. I own the first year of that decline: I moved late on the overhead.
And leaving without a role?
That is accurate. I left at the end of 2025, after the reporting line moved abroad and the mandate changed. Having said that, I would rather be honest about the timing than invent a better story.
Most people argue with me by now.
The third part is the one I would reframe. I have never lived outside Brazil, whereas I have reported to New York and to a French group for nine years.
That is a distinction I will accept. Why did you not say it first?
Because you asked in that order, and I did not want to choose the easy one first.
Yes, it fell, and I own the first year of it.
Let me reframe that, because the premise is not quite right.
It is the same answer, and I can send you the audited page today.
That is a fair question, and I have asked it myself.

When I put three hard questions together, I am not testing the answers. I already have the answers, or I would not be asking. What I am watching is the two seconds between them. Most candidates answer the first one well, and then something happens: they get faster, they get louder, or they start explaining the second one before I have finished asking it. That is the tell. The candidates who do this well are almost boring about it. They take the questions in my order, they concede what is true, they add the one thing that is also true, and then they stop and wait. Nobody has ever lost a process in my company for a decline in a margin. People lose it for what the decline does to them while they are sitting in front of me.

They asked me about the same number three times, in three different ways, and by the third time I was sure they thought I was lying. I was wrong about that. What they were doing was checking whether my answer would change under pressure, and it is a fair thing to check. The first time I gave the figure and the reason. The second time I gave exactly the same figure and the same reason, in almost the same words. The third time I said: it is the same answer, and I can send you the audited page this afternoon if that would help. The chairman laughed and moved on. I learned something that day. Under pressure, saying the same thing again, calmly, is stronger than finding a new way to say it.

Sandra asks three things at once: the margin, the eight months without a role, and never having worked abroad. Fernando says out loud that there are three parts, and takes them in her order. He concedes the fall in margin and contrasts it with the cash position. He accepts the second point as accurate, without turning it into an apology. He reframes the third one, because the premise is not quite right.
